title: A Slot in the Student Gallery

script.speaker: student
script.text: Hi. Are you the person who looks after the student gallery? I'm hoping to book a slot for the spring.

script.speaker: coordinator
script.text: That's me. Have a seat. What have you got?

script.speaker: student
script.text: It's a photography series. I've been shooting the old rail yard behind campus for about a year. I heard a slot had opened up in the main room.

script.speaker: coordinator
script.text: It did, but somebody took it on Monday. The main room's full right through to the end of term. I'm sorry.

script.speaker: student
script.text: Oh. So there's nothing left at all?

script.speaker: coordinator
script.text: I didn't say that. The corridor space is free. That's the long wall by the west stairs.

script.speaker: student
script.text: The corridor. Right. Isn't that where they put the flyers about parking?

script.speaker: coordinator
script.text: Not any more. We cleared it out last year and put in a proper hanging rail.

script.speaker: student
script.text: A rail?

script.speaker: coordinator
script.text: You can't get a nail into those walls. They're concrete behind the paint. So there's a rail along the top, and the work hangs off it on cables.

script.speaker: student
script.text: That's a problem. My whole plan was one long panorama. Three panels side by side, about twelve feet across.

script.speaker: coordinator
script.text: Then no. The cables hang straight down, so everything sits in columns. You'd want smaller prints, stacked, maybe two or three on a cable.

script.speaker: student
script.text: But the scale is the point. You're meant to stand in front of it and feel small.

script.speaker: coordinator
script.text: I know, and I'm not telling you to drop it. I'm telling you what the wall can do. Can I say one thing for the corridor?

script.speaker: student
script.text: Go ahead.

script.speaker: coordinator
script.text: Everyone walks past it. Every person heading to the lecture halls comes down those stairs. The main room's lovely, but the door's locked unless somebody's sitting in there, and most days nobody is.

script.speaker: student
script.text: So people just walk by it.

script.speaker: coordinator
script.text: They do. I've watched them. And the corridor has glass along the south side, so it's lit all day. You don't have to switch anything on.

script.speaker: student
script.text: Okay. That's not nothing. How many cables are there?

script.speaker: coordinator
script.text: Eight. They slide along the rail, so you're not stuck with even spacing.

script.speaker: student
script.text: Eight columns. I could break the panorama into a grid. It wouldn't be the same piece, but it might still work.

script.speaker: coordinator
script.text: It'd be a different piece. That isn't always a bad thing.

script.speaker: student
script.text: Can I go and look at it first, before I decide anything?

script.speaker: coordinator
script.text: Please do. It's open now. If you want the slot, fill in the request form and get it back to me by the end of next week. And bring a sketch of the layout with it. I can't approve a wall I can't picture.

script.speaker: student
script.text: Right. Which way is it from here?

script.speaker: coordinator
script.text: Out of the office and left. You can't miss it.

questions.question: What are the speakers mainly discussing?

choices.A: How the wall in the corridor by the west stairs should be repaired
choices.B: Where and in what form the student can show her photographs
choices.C: Which photographs the student ought to include in her series
choices.D: Why the main gallery room stays locked for most of the day

questions.explanation: The student states her business at the start, "I'm hoping to book a slot for the spring.", and the coordinator offers another place instead: "The corridor space is free." From then on the conversation is about how the work is hung, "the work hangs off it on cables", and how it could be arranged, "I could break the panorama into a grid." The place and the form of the exhibition are the topic from beginning to end, so the answer is B. A is wrong because repairs are never discussed. What the coordinator says, "We cleared it out last year and put in a proper hanging rail.", describes equipment that is already installed; it is not about fixing the wall. C is about choosing photographs, but which photographs to include never comes up; the talk is limited to size and arrangement. D is wrong because the locked door is mentioned only once, "the door's locked unless somebody's sitting in there", as support for the advantage of the corridor, and it is not the main topic.

questions.question: According to the coordinator, why can the student not hang her work on the corridor wall as she had planned?

choices.A: The corridor wall is too short for the panorama she has in mind
choices.B: The gallery lends out frames in one standard size only
choices.C: Another student has already reserved the corridor for the spring
choices.D: Nails will not go into the wall, so the work must hang from cables

questions.explanation: The coordinator gives the reason: "You can't get a nail into those walls. They're concrete behind the paint. So there's a rail along the top, and the work hangs off it on cables." He then explains the limit this creates, that everything lines up vertically: "The cables hang straight down, so everything sits in columns." So the answer is D. A is wrong because the length of the wall is not treated as a problem. The coordinator calls it "the long wall by the west stairs", and shortness is never given as a reason. B is wrong because frames never appear in the conversation. C is the opposite of the facts: what was taken was the slot in the main room ("somebody took it on Monday"), and about the corridor he says plainly "The corridor space is free."

questions.question: Why does the coordinator point out that the door of the main room is usually locked?

choices.A: To argue that more people would actually see the work in the corridor
choices.B: To explain how the main room came to be booked so quickly
choices.C: To warn the student that she would have to carry her own key
choices.D: To apologise for a rule that he himself does not agree with

questions.explanation: The coordinator first asks "Can I say one thing for the corridor?" and then continues, "Everyone walks past it. Every person heading to the lecture halls comes down those stairs. The main room's lovely, but the door's locked unless somebody's sitting in there, and most days nobody is." He brings up the locked main room while recommending the corridor, so his purpose is to compare how many people would see the work, which is A. B gives the wrong cause: the main room filled up because "somebody took it on Monday", a matter of who came first, and that has nothing to do with the lock. C is wrong because whether the student would carry a key is never mentioned. D is wrong because he is neither apologising nor complaining about a rule. The coordinator only uses the locked door as a weak point of the main room and gives no opinion of the rule.

questions.question: How does the student's attitude toward the corridor change during the conversation?

choices.A: She is pleased at first and then becomes worried about the cost
choices.B: She is confident at first and then doubts she can finish in time
choices.C: She treats it as second best at first and then begins to see its value
choices.D: She is unconvinced at the start and remains unconvinced at the end

questions.explanation: At first she is disappointed, "Oh. So there's nothing left at all?", and treats the corridor as a lesser place: "The corridor. Right. Isn't that where they put the flyers about parking?" But after hearing about the number of people passing and the light, she changes her attitude, "Okay. That's not nothing.", and starts working out for herself how to use it: "Eight columns. I could break the panorama into a grid." So the answer is C. A is wrong because cost is never mentioned, and she is not pleased at first either. B is wrong because whether she can finish the work in time never comes up. D contradicts the second half. Even at the end she offers to go and see the place herself, "Can I go and look at it first, before I decide anything?", so she does not stay unconvinced.

questions.question: What does the coordinator ask the student to hand in together with the request form?

choices.A: A list giving the title of each photograph in the series
choices.B: A sketch showing how the work would be laid out on the wall
choices.C: A letter of support from the teacher of her photography course
choices.D: A note stating the total weight of the panels she wants to hang

questions.explanation: At the end the coordinator says "fill in the request form and get it back to me by the end of next week. And bring a sketch of the layout with it. I can't approve a wall I can't picture." What he asks for is a drawing of the arrangement, so the answer is B. A is wrong because a list of titles does not appear in the conversation. C is wrong because neither a teacher nor a letter of support is ever mentioned. As for the weight in D, the limit the coordinator describes is "The cables hang straight down, so everything sits in columns.", which is about arrangement and not weight, and at no point does he ask for a weight figure.

questions.question: What will the student most probably do immediately after this conversation?

choices.A: Ask a different office for permission to put nails in the wall
choices.B: Abandon the panorama and start photographing a new subject
choices.C: Fill in the request form and hand it back before she leaves
choices.D: Walk over to the corridor and look at the space for herself

questions.explanation: The student asks to see the place first, "Can I go and look at it first, before I decide anything?", and the coordinator agrees: "Please do. It's open now." Finally the student asks the way, "Right. Which way is it from here?", the coordinator answers "Out of the office and left. You can't miss it.", and the conversation ends. The only place she can be heading is the corridor, so her next action is to go and look at the space, which is D. A is about asking another office to allow nails, but the student accepts the condition "You can't get a nail into those walls." and shows no sign of taking it up with anyone. B is the opposite: far from dropping her subject, she is thinking of reworking the same piece, "I could break the panorama into a grid. It wouldn't be the same piece, but it might still work." C is wrong because she herself puts off the decision with "before I decide anything", and she asks the way and leaves, so it cannot be read as handing in the form on the spot. The deadline is also still ahead: "by the end of next week".
